subject: chemistry
question_text: Discuss the application of Le Chatelier's principle for the industrial synthesis of NH₃ and SO₃.

page_header: Chemical Equilibrium, Acids and Bases · 4 marks

steps.label: Ammonia — the reaction
lines: a) Industrial synthesis of ammonia
(Haber process):
The forward reaction is exothermic, and it
reduces the gas moles from 4 to 2.
steps.why: The two facts written under the equation — exothermic, and fewer gas moles on the right — are the only inputs Le Chatelier's principle needs; every condition in the next step follows from them.
common_mistakes: Writing the equation without ΔH. The sign of ΔH is what decides the temperature condition.
Not counting the gas moles (4 on the left, 2 on the right). The count decides the pressure condition.
steps.memory_tip: Read two things off the equation: the sign of ΔH and the gas-mole count. The conditions follow.
steps.margin_note: Balanced equation with ΔH and the 4-to-2 mole count earns this mark.

steps.label: Ammonia — conditions
lines: Temperature: low temperature gives a higher
yield of NH₃ (forward reaction is
exothermic), but the reaction is then too
slow. An optimum of about 725 − 775 K is
used.
Pressure: high pressure shifts the
equilibrium to the side with fewer gas
moles, so 200 − 300 atm is used.
Catalyst: finely divided iron; promoter: Mo.
steps.why: Yield and rate ask for different temperatures — low for yield, high for speed — so industry settles on an optimum. Pressure has no such conflict: high pressure helps both.
common_mistakes: Writing simply 'low temperature is used'. The plant uses an optimum temperature because low temperature is too slow.
Leaving out the catalyst and promoter. They are part of the optimum conditions.
steps.memory_tip: Optimum temperature, high pressure, iron catalyst — the three-part answer for the Haber process.
steps.margin_note: The word optimum, with the reason for it, is what the examiner reads for.

steps.label: SO₃ — the reaction
lines: b) Industrial synthesis of SO₃
(Contact process):
This forward reaction is also exothermic,
and the gas moles decrease from 3 to 2.
steps.why: The SO₃ synthesis has the same two features as the ammonia one — exothermic and fewer gas moles on the right — so the same reasoning gives its conditions.
common_mistakes: Writing the equation unbalanced as SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ SO₃. The balanced form is 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃.
Omitting ΔH or the mole count, which the conditions are argued from.
steps.memory_tip: Same pattern as ammonia: exothermic, and 3 gas moles become 2.
steps.margin_note: Balance the equation first — 2, 1, 2 are the coefficients.

steps.label: SO₃ — conditions
lines: Temperature: low temperature gives more
SO₃ but is too slow, so an optimum of about
673 K is used.
Pressure: increase of pressure shifts the
equilibrium towards SO₃ (fewer gas moles).

lines.text: Optimum: about 673 K, 1.5 − 1.7 atm, catalyst V₂O₅

steps.why: The same yield-against-rate reasoning fixes the optimum temperature; the mole-count reasoning fixes the pressure; V₂O₅ is the named catalyst of the Contact process.
common_mistakes: Writing the Haber conditions here. The Contact process runs near 673 K and only 1.5 − 1.7 atm.
Naming iron as the catalyst. The Contact process uses V₂O₅.
steps.memory_tip: Contact process: V₂O₅ — V for vanadium, the catalyst that separates it from Haber's iron.
steps.margin_note: Temperature, pressure and catalyst for SO₃ complete the four marks.

insider_note: Both syntheses follow the same two-line logic — exothermic so an optimum temperature, fewer gas moles so raised pressure. Name the catalyst for each; that is where the last mark sits.
